result:
Solution 2 is the most plausible of the three, though I could not verify its answer of 1/3 from first principles.

- **Solution 1 (2/9)** cites a "known result" with bound (2n−5)/9 that I can't confirm. It also has no construction showing the bound is tight, so I don't trust it.
- **Solution 3 (1/4)** rests on an M₈ example that only shows λ(M₈) = 2 for one graph of 8 vertices. It doesn't give an infinite family with ratio approaching 1/4. The claimed lower bound ⌊n/4⌋ is asserted without a real proof.
- **Solution 2 (1/3)** gives a construction that does reach ratio about 1/3. Take a triangulation H on k vertices and insert a vertex into each of its 2k−4 faces, so n = 3k−4. The new vertices form an independent set, so every P₃ contains an old vertex, and λ ≤ k. Counting resources more carefully (2x + y ≤ 2k−4 new vertices, x + 2y ≤ k old vertices, with x, y the numbers of P₃s using one or two old vertices) gives λ ≈ k − 4/3 ≈ n/3. So c ≤ 1/3 for this family. Solution 2 also points to the matching bound (n+4)/3 of Biedl et al., whose tight examples have this same face-insertion form, which supports 1/3 as the natural extremal value. I did not prove that every triangulation has λ ≥ (1/3 − o(1))n, so the lower bound remains unverified.

CHOICE: 2
